answer: Before static content is moved off the application origin onto an edge/CDN host, the edge side must already own a defined set of responsibilities; the decision card makes an unowned edge configuration a hard contraindication. Concretely: (1) the publication pipeline - upload validation and version verification for each release, plus one version authority when a second origin or duplicated manifest exists; (2) the cacheability contract - an explicit cache key, freshness/lifetime policy and a controlled invalidation/purge path with a bounded stale window and propagation time, remembering that a purge lags the origin and CDN purges do not clear browser caches; (3) the authorization boundary - caching never replaces access enforcement, and changing, deleting or restricting origin content does not invalidate copies already served, so private or edge-signed assets need an explicit key and authorization contract; (4) origin protection and rewarming - prewarming critical assets per release, verifying propagation, keeping an origin failover, bounded concurrent fills, retry budgets and a deliberate stale-response policy; (5) rollback and version retention - a retained version that covers the rollback window, garbage collection only after that window, a tombstone or purge proof for a deleted object, and versioned rollback rather than mutating a cached object; and (6) accountable edge ownership per offloaded function - an owner, a versioned policy, a defined failure mode, fail-closed behavior and a tested bypass path, with acceptance tests covering the authorization matrix, purge path, stale-on-error and revocation. If edge configuration, purge or versioning cannot be owned to that standard, the design's stated alternative is to keep serving static content from the application origin.
